cells.tense: You are here at the close of something and you know it is closing.
cells.ask: Name one thing that has already finished, out loud or on paper, and say what it gave you before you move on.
cells.core:
You can feel when something is done. Not done as in ruined — done as in finished and ready to be set down. You close it without slamming it, and you don't stand around afterward trying to keep it open. When something ends on your watch, it ends, and you're still steady in the room while it does.

That steadiness is the whole thing, and it's why the next arrival can reach you. People who can't close stay crowded; there's no room for anything to land. You keep room. The ending happens, you stay open, and what's arriving gets a fair hearing instead of competing with a chapter that's still sitting in its chair.
cells.sheetLine: You can close a chapter without closing yourself.
cells.verb: closing a cycle for good and staying open to what arrives next
cells.place: in the necessary endings and the clearing that follows them

cells.tense: You will be finished with this before it is actually finished with you.
cells.ask: Look at what you're calling done and do one thing still on the table — read the last page, send the reply, ask the question.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead of you the ending already happened. You decided how this comes out, and now you're living past it — talking like it's behind you when the writing isn't finished. The bracing is real, and so is the relief you're reaching for. Neither one gets you across.

The working version is plain: a thing ends, you feel it end, and you stay open to what's next. What you're doing instead is calling it over and skipping the part where it actually closes. You won't get there by jumping the line. The real close has a few more days of work in it, and it will feel quieter than the one you're describing.

cells.tense: You kept a door open long after you had already walked through it.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're still carrying from a finished chapter and set it down in a literal place — a box, a drawer, a delete.
cells.core:
Nothing gets to be over. Something ended and you went on treating it as still live, still undecided, still possibly revivable — and that keeps the clearing from ever happening. The space is full of things you've half-left, and each one is still asking for your attention.

The finished version is simpler than it sounds: a cycle closes, you let it close, and you find out the ground is still under you. The hard part isn't knowing what ended. Somewhere in you, you do. The hard part is letting the ending count, because a finished thing can't be worked on anymore. What's arriving wants the emptied shelf, not the full one.

cells.tense: You are already in a new chapter while telling yourself you are still in the last one.
cells.ask: Say aloud one ending you have already lived through, without explaining it or softening it, and let that be true.
cells.core:
Things have closed around you and you didn't mark them. You talk about a period as ongoing when its last scene already happened — the habits changed, the people moved, the questions stopped coming. The finishing is running on its own. Your account of it hasn't caught up.

When this is balanced, you feel the close and let go without ceremony; release follows naturally because there's nothing left to hold. The gap costs you. You keep acting like you're mid-chapter, braced for something that already passed. Nothing is being asked of you here except the tally: notice what's actually over, and let that be enough to hand it over.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person has actually ended anything; Too Little may locate them at a door but not narrate what happened behind it. A reader could say 'I'm not refusing to let go, the thing genuinely isn't over,' so the ask must survive that by being about what is already here and handing over, not about enforcing an ending. The ask stays useful if the read is wrong because noticing what has already arrived still works on a live cycle. The sentence that serves me more than them is anything promising that letting go will bring relief — cut it.
